question.:question/problem:
Suppose we wish to find a zero of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[-2,0]\times [-2,0]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}xy-1 \\ {y}^{3}+3x{y}^{4}+3\end{bmatrix}. $$ Calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson process that starts with ${x}_{0}=[-1,\,-1]^{T}.$ Round your answer to three decimal places (if needed).
${x}_{1}≈$
{{field-1}}
$-0.917$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}f({x}_{n}),
$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy-1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(xy-1) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{3}+3x{y}^{4}+3) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{3}+3x{y}^{4}+3)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}y & x \\ 3{y}^{4} & 3{y}^{2}+12x{y}^{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}y & x \\ 3{y}^{4} & 3{y}^{2}+12x{y}^{3}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}xy-1 \\ {y}^{3}+3x{y}^{4}+3\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{\begin{bmatrix}y & x \\ 3{y}^{4} & 3{y}^{2}+12x{y}^{3}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}xy-1 \\ {y}^{3}+3x{y}^{4}+3\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 3(-1)^{4} & 3(-1)^{2}+12(-1)(-1)^{3}\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}(-1)(-1)-1 \\ (-1)^{3}+3(-1)(-1)^{4}+3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 3 & 15\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{(-1)\cdot 15-(-1)\cdot 3}\begin{bmatrix}15 & 1 \\ -3 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{12}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{13}{12} \\ -\frac{11}{12}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}-1.083 \\ -0.917\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

question.:question/problem:
Given the linear function $f(x; m, b) = mx + b$, compute $∇_{m, b}f$.

question.:question/worked-solution:
To compute $\nabla_{m,b}f$, we take partial derivatives with respect to $m$ and $b$.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial f}{\partial m} &=\frac{\partial}{\partial m}(mx+b)=x \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial b} &=\frac{\partial}{\partial b}(mx+b)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla_{m,b}f &=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\partial f}{\partial m} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial b}\end{bmatrix} \\ &=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Suppose we wish to find a zero of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[-3,0]\times [0,3]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}-x+{y}^{4}-3 \\ {x}^{3}-2xy+{y}^{2}+1\end{bmatrix}. $$ Calculate the second iteration of the Newton-Raphson process that starts at ${x}_{0}=[-1,\,0]^{T}$ if the first iteration of the algorithm gives ${x}_{1}=[-3,\,3]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to three decimal places (if needed).
${x}_{2}\,≈$
$-2.621$
{{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of finding the zeros of a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{n}$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{J}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}f({x}_{n}),
$$

where ${J}_{f}({x}_{n})$ is the Jacobian of $f$ evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the Jacobian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{3}-x+{y}^{4}-3) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{y}^{3}-x+{y}^{4}-3) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}-2xy+{y}^{2}+1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}-2xy+{y}^{2}+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x{y}^{3}-1 & 3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4{y}^{3} \\ 3{x}^{2}-2y & -2x+2y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}2x{y}^{3}-1 & 3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4{y}^{3} \\ 3{x}^{2}-2y & -2x+2y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}-x+{y}^{4}-3 \\ {x}^{3}-2xy+{y}^{2}+1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{\begin{bmatrix}2x{y}^{3}-1 & 3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4{y}^{3} \\ 3{x}^{2}-2y & -2x+2y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}-x+{y}^{4}-3 \\ {x}^{3}-2xy+{y}^{2}+1\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}2(-3)(3)^{3}-1 & 3(-3)^{2}(3)^{2}+4(3)^{3} \\ 3(-3)^{2}-2(3) & -2(-3)+2(3)\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}(-3)^{2}(3)^{3}-(-3)+{3}^{4}-3 \\ (-3)^{3}-2(-3)(3)+{3}^{2}+1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}-163 & 351 \\ 21 & 12\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}324 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{(-163)\cdot 12-351\cdot 21}\begin{bmatrix}12 & -351 \\ -21 & -163\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}324 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{9327}\begin{bmatrix}3537 \\ -6967\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}-2.621 \\ 2.253\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(5x{y}^{2}-5{x}^{2}-3xy-2x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(5x{y}^{2}-5{x}^{2}-3xy-2x)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-10x+5{y}^{2}-3y-2 \\ 10xy-3x\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(-10x+5{y}^{2}-3y-2) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(10xy-3x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(-10x+5{y}^{2}-3y-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(10xy-3x)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-10 & 10y-3 \\ 10y-3 & 10x\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}-10 & 10y-3 \\ 10y-3 & 10x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}-10x+5{y}^{2}-3y-2 \\ 10xy-3x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with
${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{\begin{bmatrix}-10 & 10y-3 \\ 10y-3 & 10x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}-10x+5{y}^{2}-3y-2 \\ 10xy-3x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}-10 & 10(1)-3 \\ 10(1)-3 & 10(2)\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}-10(2)+5(1)^{2}-3(1)-2 \\ 10(2)(1)-3(2)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}-10 & 7 \\ 7 & 20\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}-20 \\ 14\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{(-10)\cdot 20-7\cdot 7}\begin{bmatrix}20 & -7 \\ -7 & -10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-20 \\ 14\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{249}\begin{bmatrix}-498 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}-3{x}^{2}y-{x}^{2}-2xy+4x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}-3{x}^{2}y-{x}^{2}-2xy+4x)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x{y}^{2}-6xy-2x-2y+4 \\ 2{x}^{2}y-3{x}^{2}-2x\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2}-6xy-2x-2y+4) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}y-3{x}^{2}-2x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2}-6xy-2x-2y+4) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}y-3{x}^{2}-2x)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{y}^{2}-6y-2 & 4xy-6x-2 \\ 4xy-6x-2 & 2{x}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}2{y}^{2}-6y-2 & 4xy-6x-2 \\ 4xy-6x-2 & 2{x}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}2x{y}^{2}-6xy-2x-2y+4 \\ 2{x}^{2}y-3{x}^{2}-2x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with
${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{\begin{bmatrix}2{y}^{2}-6y-2 & 4xy-6x-2 \\ 4xy-6x-2 & 2{x}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}2x{y}^{2}-6xy-2x-2y+4 \\ 2{x}^{2}y-3{x}^{2}-2x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}2(1)^{2}-6(1)-2 & 4(1)(1)-6(1)-2 \\ 4(1)(1)-6(1)-2 & 2(1)^{2}\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}2(1)(1)^{2}-6(1)(1)-2(1)-2(1)+4 \\ 2(1)^{2}(1)-3(1)^{2}-2(1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}-6 & -4 \\ -4 & 2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{(-6)\cdot 2-(-4)\cdot (-4)}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 4 & -6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-4 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{28}\begin{bmatrix}-20 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}0.286 \\ 1.071\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be rewritten as

$$
{H}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-∇f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}y-3x{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}-2x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}y-3x{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}-2x)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8xy-3{y}^{2}+2x-2 \\ 4{x}^{2}-6xy\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(8xy-3{y}^{2}+2x-2) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}-6xy) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(8xy-3{y}^{2}+2x-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}-6xy)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8y+2 & 8x-6y \\ 8x-6y & -6x\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$
{\begin{bmatrix}8y+2 & 8x-6y \\ 8x-6y & -6x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-{\begin{bmatrix}8xy-3{y}^{2}+2x-2 \\ 4{x}^{2}-6xy\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{bmatrix}8y+2 & 8x-6y \\ 8x-6y & -6x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{\begin{bmatrix}8xy-3{y}^{2}+2x-2 \\ 4{x}^{2}-6xy\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\ \begin{bmatrix}8(1)+2 & 8(1)-6(1) \\ 8(1)-6(1) & -6(1)\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-\begin{bmatrix}8(1)(1)-3(1)^{2}+2(1)-2 \\ 4(1)^{2}-6(1)(1)\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}10 & 2 \\ 2 & -6\end{bmatrix}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system of equations, we get $({x}_{1}-{x}_{0})=\begin{bmatrix}-13/32 \\ -15/32\end{bmatrix}.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}+\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{13}{32} \\ -\frac{15}{32}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{13}{32} \\ -\frac{15}{32}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}0.594 \\ 0.531\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}y+3{x}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}y+3{x}^{2})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2{y}^{2}-2xy+6x \\ 4xy-{x}^{2}\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{y}^{2}-2xy+6x) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy-{x}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2{y}^{2}-2xy+6x) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(4xy-{x}^{2})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2y+6 & 4y-2x \\ 4y-2x & 4x\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}-2y+6 & 4y-2x \\ 4y-2x & 4x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}2{y}^{2}-2xy+6x \\ 4xy-{x}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{\begin{bmatrix}-2y+6 & 4y-2x \\ 4y-2x & 4x\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}2{y}^{2}-2xy+6x \\ 4xy-{x}^{2}\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1.75 \\ 0.125\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}-2(0.125)+6 & 4(0.125)-2(1.75) \\ 4(0.125)-2(1.75) & 4(1.75)\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}2(0.125)^{2}-2(1.75)(0.125)+6(1.75) \\ 4(1.75)(0.125)-(1.75)^{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1.75 \\ 0.125\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}5.75 & -3 \\ -3 & 7\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}10.093\,75 \\ -2.187\,5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1.75 \\ 0.125\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{(5.75)\cdot 7-(-3)\cdot (-3)}\begin{bmatrix}7 & 3 \\ 3 & 5.75\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}10.093\,75 \\ -2.187\,5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1.75 \\ 0.125\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{31.25}\begin{bmatrix}64.093\,75 \\ 17.703\,125\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}-0.301 \\ -0.442\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
$$ \left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &={x}^{2}(t)+2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=-3x(t)+{y}^{2}(t)\end{aligned}\right. $$ Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}?$
${u}^{′}=\,\,$
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}
{{field-3}}{{field-4}}
$\,\,u,\,$
where $u=x-{x}^{∗}$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\boldsymbol{f}(x)
$$

where $x=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{f}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{2}+2y \\ -3x+{y}^{2}\end{bmatrix}.$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\boldsymbol{f}(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2y)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2y)=2 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3x+{y}^{2})=-3,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3x+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}2x & 2 \\ -3 & 2y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}2(0) & 2 \\ -3 & 2(0)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ -3 & 0\end{bmatrix}u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-x+2{y}^{2})=-1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-x+2{y}^{2})=4y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-4x+{x}^{2})=-4+2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-4x+{x}^{2})=0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 4y \\ -4+2x & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ to get

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 4(0) \\ -4+2(0) & 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ -4 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ -4 & 0\end{bmatrix}u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

where $$

$$ and $$
\displaystyle \boldsymbol{f}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}4x+{y}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}-5y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\boldsymbol{f}(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\boldsymbol{f}^{′}(x)=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x+{y}^{2})=4,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x+{y}^{2})=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-5y)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-5y)=-5\end{aligned}

Thus, we have

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

where the deviation vector is

$$

To compute ${∇}_{a,b}\,f$, we take partial derivatives with respect to $a$ and $b.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂a} & =\frac{∂}{∂a}(axy+b)=xy \\ \frac{∂f}{∂b} & =\frac{∂}{∂b}(axy+b)=1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{a,b}\,f & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂a} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂b}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}xy \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

To compute ${∇}_{y,z}\,f$, we take partial derivatives with respect to $y$ and $z$ only.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}\left(\frac{xy}{z}\right) & =\frac{x}{z} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}=\frac{∂}{∂z}\left(\frac{xy}{z}\right) & =-\frac{xy}{{z}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∇}_{x,z}\,f & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2x \\ 2z\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

Next, we compute the second derivatives with respect to $x$ and $z$:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \frac{∂}{∂x}(2x)=2\,\, &  & \frac{∂}{∂z}(2x)=0 \\  & \frac{∂}{∂x}(2z)=0\,\, &  & \frac{∂}{∂z}(2z)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following:

$$

$$

knowledge_point.title: Computing One Iteration of the Newton-Raphson Method

question.:question/problem:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[-1,1]\times [-1,1]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y+3{x}^{2}-3xy+2x-{y}^{2}-5. $$ Calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization that starts at ${x}_{0}=[-1,\,-1]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to **three decimal places.**
${x}_{1}≈$
{{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}y+3{x}^{2}-3xy+2x-{y}^{2}-5) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}y+3{x}^{2}-3xy+2x-{y}^{2}-5)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4xy+6x-3y+2 \\ 2{x}^{2}-3x-2y\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(4xy+6x-3y+2) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-3x-2y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(4xy+6x-3y+2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-3x-2y)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4y+6 & 4x-3 \\ 4x-3 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}4y+6 & 4x-3 \\ 4x-3 & -2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}4xy+6x-3y+2 \\ 2{x}^{2}-3x-2y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with
${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{\begin{bmatrix}4y+6 & 4x-3 \\ 4x-3 & -2\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}4xy+6x-3y+2 \\ 2{x}^{2}-3x-2y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}4(-1)+6 & 4(-1)-3 \\ 4(-1)-3 & -2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}4(-1)(-1)+6(-1)-3(-1)+2 \\ 2(-1)^{2}-3(-1)-2(-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}2 & -7 \\ -7 & -2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{2\cdot (-2)-(-7)\cdot (-7)}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 7 \\ 7 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{53}\begin{bmatrix}43 \\ 35\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}-0.189 \\ -0.340\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Computing Two Iterations of the Newton-Raphson Method

question.:question/problem:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[-1,0]\times [0,2]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)={y}^{3}-{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}-3y. $$ Calculate the second iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization that starts at ${x}_{0}=[-1,\,2]^{T}$ if the first iteration of the algorithm gives ${x}_{1}=[-0.2,\,1.2]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to **three decimal places.**
${x}_{2}≈$
{{field-1}}
{{field-2}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{3}-{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}-3y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{3}-{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}-3y)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2xy-4x \\ 3{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}-3\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2xy-4x) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(3{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}-3) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(-2xy-4x) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(3{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}-3)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2y-4 & -2x \\ -2x & 6y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}-2y-4 & -2x \\ -2x & 6y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}-2xy-4x \\ 3{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}-3\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

For the second iteration, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={x}_{1}-{\begin{bmatrix}-2y-4 & -2x \\ -2x & 6y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}-2xy-4x \\ 3{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}-3\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{1}} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-0.2 \\ 1.2\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}-2(1.2)-4 & -2(-0.2) \\ -2(-0.2) & 6(1.2)\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}-2(-0.2)(1.2)-4(-0.2) \\ 3(1.2)^{2}-(-0.2)^{2}-3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-0.2 \\ 1.2\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}-6.4 & 0.4 \\ 0.4 & 7.2\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}1.28 \\ 1.28\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-0.2 \\ 1.2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{(-6.4)\cdot 7.2-0.4\cdot 0.4}\begin{bmatrix}7.2 & -0.4 \\ -0.4 & -6.4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1.28 \\ 1.28\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-0.2 \\ 1.2\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{46.24}\begin{bmatrix}8.704 \\ -8.704\end{bmatrix} \\  & ≈\begin{bmatrix}-0.012 \\ 1.012\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Next, we compute the second derivatives with respect to $y$ and $z$:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}z)=0\,\, &  & \frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}z)={x}^{2} \\  & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y)={x}^{2}\,\, &  & \frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}y)=0\end{aligned}

$$

$$
